heading: 2.8.1 Simple example
text:
Consider rolling standard, fair six-sided die.
Define \(\) set numbers can rolled die, \(B\) set even numbers can rolled,  \(C\) numbers can rolled divisible three.R can used determine elements sets, union intersection sets.First, define sets:use R find intersection union:function setdiff() finds difference two sets:.element(, B) determines elements  \(\) contained set \(B\):
code:
Die_Rolls <- 1:6 # Set A
Rolls_Even <- seq(2, 6, by = 2)    # Set B
Rolls_Divisible_By_3 <- c(3, 6)    # Set C
Rolls_Even                         # Set B
#> [1] 2 4 6
Rolls_Divisible_By_3               # Set C
#> [1] 3 6
intersect(Rolls_Even, Rolls_Divisible_By_3)
#> [1] 6
union(Rolls_Even, Rolls_Divisible_By_3)
#> [1] 2 4 6 3
sort( union(Rolls_Even, Rolls_Divisible_By_3) )
#> [1] 2 3 4 6
setdiff(Rolls_Even, Rolls_Divisible_By_3)  # B \ C
#> [1] 2 4
setdiff(Rolls_Divisible_By_3, Rolls_Even)  # C \ B: not symmetric!
#> [1] 3
is.element(Rolls_Divisible_By_3, Rolls_Even)  # The two elements of A
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE
is.element(Rolls_Even, Rolls_Divisible_By_3)  # The three elements of B
#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE

code:
P_cancer <- function(population_Size = 10000,   # Population size
                     cancer_Prob = 0.02,        # Pr(really has cancer)
                     sensitivity = 0.75,        # Pr(+ive test | has cancer)
                     specificity = 0.90) {      # Pr(-ive test | no cancer)
  
  # True cancer status: Generate a random number for each person. 
  # People with a number less than the 'threshold' have cancer.
  cancer <- runif(population_Size) < cancer_Prob
     # cancer  is a vector of TRUE and FALSE values.
     # runif(population_Size) produces that many random numbers between 0 & 1
  
  # Test results: Create a logical vector (empty for now)
  # to fill with TRUE or FALSE as appropriate.
  test_positive <- logical(population_Size)
  
  # Sensitivity: P(test positive | cancer)
  # * sum(cancer) is the number of people truly with cancer
  # * runif( sum(cancer) ) produces that many random numbers
  # * if that random number is less than 'sensitivity': positive test
  test_positive[cancer] <- runif(sum(cancer)) < sensitivity
  
  # False positive rate: 1 - specificity
  # * sum(!cancer) is the number of people truly without cancer
  # * runif( sum(!cancer) ) produces that many random numbers
  # * if that random number is less than '1-specificity': positive test
  test_positive[!cancer] <- runif(sum(!cancer)) < (1 - specificity)
  
  # Compute P(Cancer | Test positive)
  # Have to be careful: If there are no positive test results,
  # we will end up dividing by zero...
  if (sum(test_positive) == 0) return(NA)  # NA: not available
  
  mean(cancer[test_positive])
}
P_cancer()        # This uses all the default values
#> [1] 0.1418248

                     P_cancer())    # ... using this function

mean(results, na.rm = TRUE)     # na.rm = TRUE ignores any NAs
#> [1] 0.1328612
sd(results, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 0.01004723

set.seed(8723) # Set the random number seed, for reproducibility

num_Reps <- 5000  # Set the number of simulations

# 'Name' the 10 people by using the 'initials' of the ten people
People <- LETTERS[1:10] # The first 10 capital letters: the people
People
#>  [1] "A" "B" "C" "D" "E" "F" "G" "H" "I" "J"
# The function takes a seating arrangement as input, given as (for example) 
# "A", "J", "F", "G", "H", "I", "E", "B", "G", "J", "C", "D"
#
# It checks, for any given seating arrangement, if "A" and "B" are neighbours.

check_If_Neighbours <- function(Arrangement) {
  n <- length(Arrangement)
  
  # Allow for circular adjacency: append first element at the end
  extended <- c(Arrangement, Arrangement[1])
  
  # Compare each person with the next
  right <- extended[-1]            # right: positions 2... (n+1)
  left  <- extended[-(n + 1)]      # current: positions 1... n
  
  # Check if A next to B, or if B next to A
  are_Neighbours <- any((left == "A" & right == "B") | 
                        (left == "B" & right == "A"))
  
  return(are_Neighbours)
}
# Run simulation
# Summing works, because  TRUE  is treated as 1, FALSE  is treated as 0
seated_Together <- sum( replicate(num_Reps, 
                                  check_If_Neighbours( sample(People))) )
# sample(People) makes a random arrangement of the 10 people
# Estimated probability
prob <- seated_Together / num_Reps
cat("Prob. of an UNacceptable seating arrangement: approx. ", 
    round(prob, 4), "\n") # Round to four decimal places
#> Prob. of an UNacceptable seating arrangement: approx.  0.216

expected value  \(U\) 
\[\begin{align*}

expected value  \(X\) 
\[\begin{align*}
   \operatorname{E}[X]
   &= \int_{-\infty}^\infty x\, f_X(x) \, dx

expected value  \(X\) \(\operatorname{E}[X] = 13/6\).Example 6.3  (Expectation mixed variables) Consider continuous random variable \(W\) probability function

\end{align*}\]

heading: 6.7 Tchebysheff’s inequality
text:
Tchebysheff’s inequality applies probability distribution, sometimes useful theoretical work provide bounds probabilities.Theorem 6.8  (Tchebysheff's theorem) Let \(X\) random variable finite mean \(\mu\) variance \(\sigma^2\).
positive \(k\),
\[\begin{equation}
   \Pr\big(|X - \mu| \geq k\sigma \big)\leq \frac{1}{k^2}
   \tag{6.5}
\end{equation}\]
, equivalently
\[\begin{equation}
   \Pr\big(|X - \mu| < k\sigma \big)\geq 1 - \frac{1}{k^2}.
\end{equation}\]Proof. proof continuous case given.
Let \(X\) continuous PDF \(f(x)\).
\(c > 0\), 
\[\begin{align*}
     \sigma^2
     & = \int^\infty_{-\infty} (x - \mu )^2f(x)\,dx\\
     & = \int^{\mu -\sqrt{c}}_{-\infty} (x - \mu )^2f(x)\, dx +
         \int^{\mu + \sqrt{c}}_{\mu-\sqrt{c}}(x - \mu )^2f(x)\,dx +
         \int^\infty_{\mu + \sqrt{c}}(x - \mu)^2f(x)\,dx\\
     & \geq \int^{\mu -\sqrt{c}}_{-\infty} (x - \mu )^2f(x)\,dx +
       \int^\infty_{\mu + \sqrt{c}}(x - \mu )^2f(x)\,dx,
\end{align*}\]
since second integral non-negative.
Now \((x - \mu )^2 \geq c\) \(x \leq \mu -\sqrt{c}\) \(x\geq \mu + \sqrt{c}\).
remaining integrals , replace \((x - \mu )^2\) \(c\) without altering direction inequality:
\[\begin{align*}
  \sigma^2
  &\geq  c \int^{\mu -\sqrt{c}}_{-\infty} f(x)\,dx + c\int^\infty_{\mu + \sqrt{c}}f(x)\,dx\\
  &=  c\,\Pr(X \leq \mu - \sqrt{c}\,) + c\,\Pr(X \geq \mu + \sqrt{c}\,)\\
  &=  c\,\Pr(|X - \mu| \geq \sqrt{c}\,).
\end{align*}\]
Putting \(\sqrt{c} = k\sigma\), Eq. (6.5) obtained.probability function PDF random variable \(X\), \(\operatorname{E}[X]\) \(\operatorname{var}[X]\) can found, converse true.
, knowledge \(\operatorname{E}[X]\) \(\operatorname{var}[X]\) reconstruct probability distribution  \(X\) hence compute probabilities \(\Pr(|X - \mu| \geq k\sigma)\).
Nonetheless, using Tchebysheff’s inequality can find useful bound either probability outside inside \(\mu \pm k\sigma\).

\[
      p_U(u) = \begin{cases}

\]

\[\begin{align*}

      &= p_{U, V}(u,v)/p_{U}(u = 11) \\
      &= \begin{cases}
             \frac{1/18}{7/18} = 1/7 & \text{$v = 0$};\\
             \frac{1/3}{7/18}  = 6/7 & \text{$v = 1$}
          \end{cases}
   \end{align*}\]
using \(p_U(u = 11) = 7/18\) Step 1.Thirdly, find conditional mean:
\[
  \operatorname{E}[V\mid U = 11]
  = \sum_v v p_{V\mid U}(v\mid u = 11)
  = \left(\frac{1}{7}\times 0\right) + \left(\frac{6}{7}\times 1\right)

\]
Fourthly, find conditional second raw moment:
\[
  \operatorname{E}[V^2\mid U]
  = \sum_v v^2 p_{V\mid U}(v\mid u = 11)
  = \left(\frac{1}{7}\times 0^2\right) + \left(\frac{6}{7}\times 1^2\right)

\[\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{var}[V\mid U = 11]
  &= \operatorname{E}[V\mid U = 11] - (\operatorname{E}[V\mid U = 11])^2\\
  &= (6/7) - (6/7)^2\\

\end{align*}\]

code:
### Define the function, without the constant term
g <- function(x){
  ifelse(x > 0, 
         x^(-0.5) * exp(-x - sqrt(2 * x)), # When x > 0
         0)                                # When x <= 0
}

### Integrate between 0 and infinity:
#\n adds a "new line"
Const <- 1 / integrate(g, 
                       lower = 0, 
                       upper = Inf)$value
cat("The value of  c  is about", round(Const, 4), "\n")
#> The value of  c  is about 1.0784

# So now define f(x):
f <- function(x){
  ifelse(x > 0, 
         x^(-0.5) * exp(-x - sqrt(2 * x)) * Const,  # When x > 0
         0)                                         # When x <= 0
}
F <- function(x){
  F <- array(dim = length(x) )
  for (i in 1:length(x)){
    F[i] <- integrate( f, 
                       lower = 0,
                       upper = x[i])$value
  }
  return(F)
}
### Make room for two plots side-by-side
par( mfrow = c(1, 2))

### Evaluate over these values of x
x <- seq(0.01, 2, 
         length = 1000)

### Now plot
plot( f(x) ~ x,
      type = "l",
      las = 1,
      lwd = 3,
      main = "Density function",
      xlab = expression(italic(x)),
      ylab = "Density fn.")
plot( F(x) ~ x,
      type = "l",
      las = 1,
      lwd = 3,
      main = "Distribution function",
      xlab = expression(italic(x)),
      ylab = "Distribution fn.")
integrate(f,
          lower = 0.5,
          upper = Inf)
#> 0.1433935 with absolute error < 4.4e-06
f_Expected <- function(x){
  x * f(x)
}
integrate(f_Expected, 
          lower = 0,
          upper = Inf)
#> 0.2374324 with absolute error < 2.1e-07

       \frac{ \binom{13}{5} \binom{7}{0}}{ \binom{20}{5} } \\
   & \approx  0.3228 + 0.0830 = 0.4058.
\end{align*}\]

\[

\(|J|\) absolute value Jacobian determinant:
\[
  J = \det
        \begin{bmatrix}
          {\partial x_1}/{\partial y_1} &  {\partial x_1}/{\partial y_2} \\

\[
  f_X(x) = \exp(-x)\quad\text{$x > 0$}.
\]
Consider two transformations \(Y_1 = X_1 + X_2\) (sum) \(Y_2 = X_1 / X_2\) (ratio).
, \(y_1 > 0\) \(y_2 > 0\).Since random variable \(X_1\)  \(X_2\) independent, joint PDF 
\[
  f_{X_1, X_2}(x_1, x_2) = \exp(-x_1) \cdot \exp(-x_2) = \exp\left(-(x_1 + x_2)\right) \quad \text{$x_1, x_2 > 0$}.
\]
Inverting transformations gives \(y_1 = x_1 + x_2\) \(y_2 = x_1 / x_2\) (\(x_1 = y_2 x_2\)).
give
\[
  x_1 = \frac{y_1 y_2}{1 + y_2}
  \quad\text{}\quad
  x_2 = \frac{y_1}{1 + y_2}.
\]
Jacobian requires four partial derivatives:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
  \displaystyle \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial y_1} = \frac{y_2}{1+y_2};\quad & \quad\displaystyle \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial y_2} = \frac{y_1(1+y_2) - y_1 y_2}{(1+y_2)^2} = \frac{y_1}{(1+y_2)^2};\\[6pt]
  \displaystyle \frac{\partial x_2}{\partial y_1} = \frac{1}{1+y_2};\quad & \quad\displaystyle \frac{\partial x_2}{\partial y_2} = \frac{-y_1}{(1+y_2)^2}.
\end{array}
\]
determinant Jacobian 
\[\begin{align*}
  \det J
  &= \left( \frac{y_2}{1+y_2} \cdot \frac{-y_1}{(1+y_2)^2} \right) - \left( \frac{1}{1+y_2} \cdot \frac{y_1}{(1+y_2)^2} \right)\\
  &= \frac{-y_1 y_2 - y_1}{(1+y_2)^3}\\
  &= \frac{-y_1(y_2 + 1)}{(1+y_2)^3}.
\end{align*}\]
Finally, substitute \(x_1\)  \(x_2\)  \(|J|\) formula:
\[
  f_{Y_1, Y_2}(y_1, y_2) = \exp(-(x_1 + x_2)) \cdot \left| \frac{-y_1}{(1 + y_2)^2} \right|.
\]
Since \(x_1 + x_2 = y_1\), write
\[
  f_{Y_1, Y_2}(y_1, y_2) = \frac{y_1 \exp(-y_1)}{(1+y_2)^2}\quad\text{$y_1 > 0$ $y_2 > 0$}.
\]

heading: 11.4 Joint probability functions
text:
joint probability function \(\mathbf{X}\) describes probability distribution \(n\) random variables simultaneously.Definition 11.1  (Joint probability function (discrete)) Let \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \dots, X_n)\) \(n\)-dimensional discrete random variable.
random variable \(X_j\) (\(j = 1, \dots, n\)) takes values set \(S_j\) (range)., range random vector 
\[
  \mathcal{X} \subseteq S_1\times \cdots \times S_n.
\]
, joint probability mass function 
\[
  p_{X_1, \dots, X_n}(x_1, \dots, x_n)
  = \Pr(X_1 = x_1,\, \dots,\, X_n = x_n) \quad \text{$(x_1, \dots, x_n) \\mathcal{X}$},
\]

\[
  p_{X_1, \dots, X_n}(x_1, \dots, x_n) \geq 0
  \quad \text{$(x_1, \dots, x_n) \\mathcal{X}$},
\]

\[
  \sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_n) \\mathcal{X}} p_{X_1, \dots, X_n}(x_1, \dots, x_n) = 1.
\]Example 11.1  (Three dice) Consider random vector \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, X_2, X_3)\) representing outcome rolling three fair six-sided dice.Since \(X_j \\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\), range 
\[
  \mathcal{X} = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\} \times \{1,2,3,4,5,6\} \times \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}.
\]
Assuming dice independent, joint probabuility mass function 
\[\begin{align*}
  p_{X_1, X_2, X_3}(x_1, x_2, x_3)
  &=
  \Pr(X_1 = x_1, X_2 = x_2, X_3 = x_3)\\
  &= \frac{1}{6^3} = \frac{1}{216}
\end{align*}\]
\((x_1, x_2, x_3) \\mathcal{X}\).instance, probability sum three dice equals \(10\) 
\[
  \Pr(X_1 + X_2 + X_3 = 10)
  = \sum_{\substack{(x_1, x_2, x_3) \\mathcal{X}\\ x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 10}} p(x_1,x_2,x_3).
\]obtain answer R, use:case continuous random variables, definition similar.Definition 11.2  (Joint probability function (continuous)) Let \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \dots, X_n)\) \(n\)-dimensional continuous random vector.
\(j = 1, \dots, n\), random variable \(X_j\) takes values subset \(S_j \subseteq \mathbb{R}\).range vector therefore
\[
  \mathcal{X} \subseteq S_1 \times \cdots \times S_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n.
\]
joint probability density function \(\mathbf{X}\) 
\[
  f_{X_1, \dots, X_n}(x_1, \dots, x_n), \quad \text{$(x_1, \dots, x_n) \\mathcal{X}$},
\]

\[
  f_{X_1, \dots, X_n}(x_1, \dots, x_n) \geq 0
  \quad \text{$(x_1, \dots, x_n) \\mathcal{X}$},
\]

\[
  \int_{\mathcal{X}} f_{X_1, \dots, X_n}(x_1, \dots, x_n)\, dx_1 \cdots dx_n = 1.
\]Example 11.2  (Three-dimensional uniform example (continuous)) Consider random vector \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, X_2, X_3)\), uniformly distributed unit cube \([0, 1]^3\).
range 
\[
  \mathcal{X} = [0, 1] \times [0, 1] \times [0, 1] \subset \mathbb{R}^3.
\]joint probability density function :
\[
  f_{X_1, X_2, X_3}(x_1,x_2,x_3) =
  \begin{cases}
    1 & \text{$0 \le x_j \le 1$ $j = 1, 2, 3$},\\
    0 & \text{otherwise}.
  \end{cases}
\]marginal distributions uniform \([0, 1]\); example:
\[
  f_{X_1}(x_1) = \int_0^1 \int_0^1 f(x_1, x_2, x_3)\, dx_2\, dx_3 = 1, \quad 0\le x_1 \le 1.
\]instance, probability sum three variables less equal  \(1\) 
\[
  \Pr(X_1 + X_2 + X_3 \le 1)
  = \text{volume tetrahedron } \{(x_1,x_2,x_3)\\mathcal{X}: x_1 + x_2 + x_3 \le 1\}
  = \frac{1}{6}.

heading: 12.1 Expectation
text:
Results involving expectations naturally generalise bivariate multivariate case.
Firstly, expectation linear combination random variables.Theorem 12.1  (Expectation linear combinations) \(X_1, X_2,\dots, X_n\) random variables \(a_1, a_2,\ldots a_n\) constants 
\[
   \operatorname{E}\left[\sum_{= 1}^n a_i X_i \right]
   =\sum_{= 1}^n a_i \, \operatorname{E}[X_i]
\]Proof. proof follows directly Theorem 6.9 induction.variance linear combination random variables given following theorem.Theorem 12.2  (Variance linear combination) \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\) random variables \(a_1, a_2,\ldots a_n\) constants 
\[
   \operatorname{var}\left[\sum_{= 1}^n a_i X_i \right]
   =
   \sum^n_{= 1}^2_i\operatorname{var}[X_i] + 2{\sum\sum}_{<j}a_i a_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i, X_j).
\]Proof. convenience, put \(Y = \sum_{= 1}^n a_iX_i\).
definition variance
\[\begin{align*}
     \operatorname{var}[Y]
     &= \operatorname{E}\big[Y - \operatorname{E}(Y)\big]^2\\
     &= \operatorname{E}[a_1 X_1 + \dots + a_n X_n - a_1\mu_1 - \dots a_n\mu_n]^2\\
     &= \operatorname{E}[a_1(X_1 - \mu_1) + \dots + a_n(X_n - \mu_n)]^2\\
     &= \operatorname{E}\left[ \sum_i ^2_i(X_i - \mu_i)^2 + 2\mathop{\sum\sum}_{< j}a_i a_j(X_i - \mu_i)X_j - \mu_j)\right]\\
     &= \sum_i ^2_i\operatorname{E}[X_i - \mu_i]^2 + 2\mathop{\sum\sum}_{< j}a_i a_j\operatorname{E}[X_i - \mu_i] (X_j - \mu_j)\\
        %\quad \text{using Theorem\ \@ref(thm:ExpLinear)}\\
     &= \sum_i ^2_i\sigma^2_i + 2\mathop{\sum\sum}_{<j}a_i a_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i, X_j).
\end{align*}\]statistical theory, important special case Theorem 12.2 occurs  \(X_i\) independently identically distributed (IID).
, \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\) distribution independent .

text:

\[\begin{equation}

\[\begin{align*}

    &= \frac{1}{n} \left( \sigma^2 + \sigma^2 + \cdots + \sigma^2 \right)\\
    &= \frac{1}{n} \times n\sigma^2 = \sigma^2.
\end{align*}\]

heading: 13.8 The normal approximation to the binomial
text:
normal approximation binomial distribution (Sect. 8.3.5 can seen application Central Limit Theorem.
essential observation sample proportion sample mean.
Consider sequence independent Bernoulli trials resulting random sample \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\) 
\[
  X_i
  =
  \begin{cases}
     0  &  \text{failure}\\
     1  &  \text{success}
  \end{cases}
\]
denotes whether \(\)th trial success.
sum
\[
   Y = \sum_{= 1}^n X_i
\]
represents number successes \(n\) trials 
\[
   \bar{X}
   =
   \frac{1}{n}\sum_{= 1}^n X_i
   =
   \frac{Y}{n}
\]
sample mean representing proportion fraction trials successful.
context, \(\bar{X}\) usually denoted sample proportion \(\widehat{p}\).Note \(\operatorname{E}[X_i] = p\) \(\operatorname{var}[X_i] = p(1 - p)\).
Therefore
\[
   \operatorname{E}[Y] = np
   \quad\text{}\quad
   \operatorname{var}[Y] = np(1 - p)
\]

\[
   \operatorname{E}[\bar{X}] = p
   \quad\text{}\quad
   \operatorname{var}[\bar{X}] = \frac{p(1 - p)}{n}.
\]
Theorems 13.16  13.17 applicable  \(\bar{X}\)  \(Y\) respectively.
Hence
\[
   \bar{X} = \widehat{p}
   \sim N\left(p, \frac{p(1 - p)}{n}\right)\text{ approximately}
\]

\[
   Y = n\widehat{p}
   \sim N(np, np(1 - p))\text{ approximately}.
\]

\[\begin{align}

\[\begin{align}

\end{align}\]

# Set the number of simulations
num_simulations <- 100000

# Initialize a vector to store the number of rolls required for each simulation
rolls_required <- integer(num_simulations)

# Function to simulate rolling a die until the total is exactly 4
simulate_rolls <- function() {
  total <- 0
  rolls <- 0
  while (total < 4) {
    roll <- sample(1:6, 1) # Roll the die
    total <- total + roll
    rolls <- rolls + 1
    if (total > 4) {
      return(NA) # Return NA if the total exceeds 4
    }
  }
  return(rolls)
}

# Perform simulations
for (i in 1:num_simulations) {
  result <- simulate_rolls()
  if (!is.na(result)) {
    rolls_required[i] <- result
  }
}

# Remove NA values from the results
rolls_required <- na.omit(rolls_required)

# Remove zero values (impossible cases)
rolls_required <- rolls_required[rolls_required > 0]

# Calculate the PMF
PMF <- table(rolls_required) / length(rolls_required)

# Print the PMF
print(PMF)

# Optionally, plot the PMF
barplot(PMF, main="Probability Mass Function of Rolls Needed to Sum to 4",
        xlab="Number of Rolls", ylab="Probability",
        col="lightblue", border="blue")
